items.prompt: A team designs every possible future option before writing any code. Which posture is this?
choices: Big upfront design
Evolutionary design
Rewrite on every change
items.explanation: Designing everything before any code exists is upfront design.

items.prompt: A team deletes the working checkout and starts over each time a rule is added. Which posture is this?
choices: Big upfront design of the whole system
Rewrite on every change
Evolutionary design
items.explanation: Starting over for each change is the rewrite posture.

items.prompt: Which posture reshapes the design only when a real requirement arrives?
choices: Big upfront design
Rewrite on every change
Evolutionary design
items.explanation: Reacting to requirements that actually arrived is the evolutionary posture.

items.prompt: What must big upfront design assume?
choices: It can guess every way the system will change
Requirements never change after launch
Rewriting is always cheaper than editing
items.explanation: Upfront design is a bet on predictions, and some predictions will be wrong.

items.prompt: What is thrown away when a team rewrites from scratch for each new rule?
choices: The need to ever write tests again
Working code that is already tested
Every customer's saved account data
items.explanation: Rewrites discard logic that already works and was already tested.

items.prompt: What is the goal of evolutionary design?
choices: No future change ever needs a code edit
Every future change is predicted today
Each change costs about as much as the last
items.explanation: It aims to keep the cost of change roughly flat, not to remove change.

items.prompt: Why does big upfront design often waste effort?
choices: Unused flexibility still has to be maintained
Flexible code always runs slower than plain code
Teams cannot write plans for software
items.explanation: Flexibility nobody uses still has to be read, tested and kept up.

items.prompt: A shop's checkout has one discount rule and no abstraction. Is that a sound evolutionary start?
choices: No, every checkout needs a rules framework first
Yes, it reshapes once a real second rule appears
No, one rule always demands a full rewrite
items.explanation: One rule needs no structure; the second real rule is the signal to reshape.

items.prompt: Three teams meet a new discount request. Team A builds a plug-in framework for every discount it can imagine. Team B deletes the checkout and rewrites it. Team C adds the rule and reshapes only the part that became awkward. Which one is practising evolutionary design?
choices: Team C: it reshapes only the awkward part, driven by a requirement that arrived
Team A: it prepared for every change in the whole system before any change had arrived
Team B: it starts clean every time, so no old design constrains it ever
None of them: evolving a design means never touching existing code at all
items.explanation: Team C changes structure in response to a real requirement and keeps the working code. Team A is upfront design; Team B is rewriting.
items.reference:
Three ways to meet change
upfront: guess every axis today
rewrite: start over each time
evolutionary: reshape when a real need arrives
Why: only the third keeps each change about as cheap as the last.
items.learnMore:
Three postures toward change

Upfront design bets on predictions, rewriting discards tested work, and evolutionary design reshapes structure only in response to requirements that actually arrived.

Common mistake

Treating evolutionary design as hacking. It still reshapes the structure, just when evidence arrives.
items.reflection: Think of a household or team routine that you redesigned only after a second real problem showed up. What did the first problem alone not justify?

items.prompt: A rewrite on every change feels clean at first. Why does it get worse as the system grows?
choices: New code is always less readable than the code it replaces, at any size
Re-deriving and re-testing everything costs more each time, and lessons are lost
Rewrites become forbidden once more than one customer uses the system
Each rewrite must also rewrite the tests, which can never be automated
items.explanation: The work to redo grows with the system, and the old code's tested behaviour is discarded rather than reused.

items.prompt: A plan says: predict all pricing changes for two years and build for them now. Six months in, only half of the predicted axes have appeared. What is the main cost?
choices: The used half stops working because the unused half shares its code
No rule outside the original prediction list can ever be added again
The unused half still has to be read, tested and kept up for nothing
Nothing, since flexibility that goes unused is removed automatically
items.explanation: Speculative flexibility is paid for continuously whether or not it is ever used.

items.prompt: Which statement best separates evolutionary design from just hacking each rule in?
choices: It adds more code up front than hacking does so later changes are faster
It forbids special cases entirely, while hacking allows any number of them
It uses diagrams to plan every change, while hacking skips documentation
It reshapes once a second real case shows up; hacking just keeps stacking
items.explanation: The difference is the reshaping step. Evolutionary design stops stacking at the point where stacking begins to cost more than structure.

items.prompt: Open for extension, closed for modification means you can...
choices: add behaviour without editing existing tested code
edit any code at any time without testing
never add behaviour to a finished module
items.explanation: The point is to add new behaviour while leaving working code alone.

items.prompt: After the seam exists, a new pricing rule is added by...
choices: editing the body of the checkout function
appending a new item to the rule list
rewriting every earlier rule from scratch
items.explanation: The checkout function stays untouched; the list grows.

items.prompt: What does the checkout function look like once the seam is in place?
choices: It checks each rule by name in a long chain
It is rewritten each time a rule is added
It loops over whatever rules it is given
items.explanation: It holds no rule-specific logic, only the loop.

items.prompt: What is one cost of the rule-list seam?
choices: One more concept to learn and one more hop to read
Every rule must be rewritten each round
The checkout can no longer be tested at all
items.explanation: Indirection is the price: a shared shape plus a list to look up.

items.prompt: What does the seam buy?
choices: Rules never need their own tests ever again, once listed
New rules cannot break old rules' tested behaviour
The total no longer depends on rule order
items.explanation: Old rules are untouched, so their tested behaviour is protected. Order still matters.

items.prompt: Is open-closed a free win with no price?
choices: Yes, because it only ever removes code from the whole system
Yes, indirection is always free for the reader
No, it adds a shared shape and a layer of indirection
items.explanation: It is a trade: protection from edits against a bit more to read.

items.prompt: When is open-closed worth its price?
choices: When editing costs more than reading one extra interface
Whenever the team has time to add a new file to the project
Only in systems that are certain to ever have just one rule
items.explanation: The crossover point is the judgment: editing cost against reading cost.

items.prompt: Which part is closed for modification after round 2?
choices: The rule list, which can never grow again
The checkout function that runs the rules
The tax rate, which can never change again
items.explanation: The function that loops over rules stays fixed while the list is open to additions.

items.prompt: A reviewer says the seam made the code worse because you now open two places to see what a total includes. Which reply is accurate?
choices: True, that is the price; it pays off when editing becomes costlier
False, a seam never adds anything the reader has to look up first
True, so the seam should be removed as soon as the bug is fixed
False, readers should trust the rule names and skip reading the list
items.explanation: The extra hop is a real cost. It is justified when the alternative, editing a crowded function, costs more.
items.reference:
Open-closed, as a ledger
bought: new rules cannot disturb tested old rules
paid: one extra shape, one extra list, one more hop
worth it when editing a crowded function costs more
Why: it is a trade with a price, not a free win.
items.learnMore:
What closed for modification buys

After the seam exists, the checkout function only loops over the rules it is given. A new rule is an addition, so existing rules and their tests stay as they were.

Common mistake

Calling it free. The extra shape and the extra place to read are a real cost, paid every day.
items.reflection: Think of a shared checklist or template you add to rather than rewrite. What would it cost you to keep it that way, and when did it start to pay for itself?

items.prompt: Which change breaks closed-for-modification in the rule-list design?
choices: Appending a new rule object to the end of the rule list
Adding an if-branch for the new rule inside the checkout function
Writing a new unit test for the newest rule in the list
Reading the rule list to find which rules apply to an order
items.explanation: Editing the checkout function's body is modification. Appending to the list and testing are extension.

items.prompt: At round 1 the team has one discount rule. Is a rule-list seam justified?
choices: No, there is no second rule yet
Yes, because more rules might come later
Yes, because every function should have one
items.explanation: With one rule there is no evidence the axis will vary.

items.prompt: What does YAGNI stand for?
choices: You Always Get New Items
You Aren't Gonna Need It
You Aim to Grow Nightly
items.explanation: It warns against building for requirements that have not arrived.

items.prompt: Which is evidence of a real axis of change?
choices: A teammate feels more rules will come someday
The product might one day run in other countries
A second rule arrived and collided with the first
items.explanation: An actual second rule is evidence. Feelings and possibilities are not.

items.prompt: No customer has asked for other currencies. Is multi-currency pricing a real axis today?
choices: No, it is speculation
Yes, because every shop needs it eventually
Yes, but only for large orders over $500
items.explanation: Without evidence, currency is an imagined axis.

items.prompt: What does a seam for an axis that never moves cost?
choices: Nothing, since unused code costs no time
Indirection paid every day with no payoff
A full rewrite of the original checkout
items.explanation: Unused structure still has to be read and kept up.

items.prompt: YAGNI and design-for-change seem opposed. The skill is to choose...
choices: one of them and ignore the other entirely
the axis that sounds the most important
which axis has real evidence of change now
items.explanation: Evidence picks the axis; the two ideas then work together.

items.prompt: Round 2 brought a second rule that caused a bug. What does that change?
choices: It turns a hypothetical axis into a confirmed one
It proves that new rules should never be added again to it
It makes tax rates the next likely axis
items.explanation: The collision is real evidence that the rule axis varies.

items.prompt: 'We obviously know more rules are coming.' What kind of reasoning is this?
choices: Hard evidence gathered from the present system
A guess about the future, not evidence
A formal requirement from a customer
items.explanation: It predicts rather than observes, so it is speculation.

items.prompt: A team lists four possible axes of change. Which one has real evidence?
choices: Rules: a second discount rule shipped last week and collided with the first
Currencies: sales says a foreign customer is probably coming sometime this year
Tax: the founder thinks regional taxes will matter once the firm is bigger
Plans: a competitor recently launched a monthly billing plan of its own
items.explanation: Only the first is something that actually happened inside this system.
items.reference:
Evidence or guess?
evidence: a second rule arrived and collided with the first
guess: a customer abroad is probably coming
guess: the company will probably grow into new regions
Why: a seam for an axis that never moves is cost with no payoff.
items.learnMore:
Signal versus speculation

YAGNI and design-for-change stop conflicting once you ask which axis has real evidence of moving. Protect that axis; leave the others alone until they show evidence too.

Common mistake

Treating a confident feeling as evidence. A certain-feeling guess costs the same to carry as a wrong one.
items.reflection: Think of a purchase or preparation you made for a future that never came. What would have counted as evidence beforehand, as opposed to a feeling?

items.prompt: A teammate says: we will definitely need the abstraction eventually, so build it now. What is the flaw?

Teammates are never right about the future, so predictions are always ignored

items.prompt: When should the seam be introduced?
choices: When a second variant of the same kind arrives
At round 1, before any rule exists
Never, since plain ifs always scale fine
items.explanation: The second variant is the signal.

items.prompt: What is 'too early' for a seam?
choices: Building it right after the second rule arrives
Building it for an axis with no second variant
Building it after the first bug report
items.explanation: Too early means paying for structure that is never used twice.

items.prompt: What is 'too late'?
choices: Adding the first and only rule in round one
Never adding any further rules to the checkout at all
Stacking more ifs after the second caused a bug
items.explanation: Waiting past the second variant lets interactions pile up.

items.prompt: A VIP discount arrives, the same kind as the existing rules. What goes in?
choices: Append it to the existing rule list
Build a second seam just for VIP
Add an if-branch inside checkout
items.explanation: Same kind of thing, so the existing seam covers it.

items.prompt: A regional tax rate changes how tax is computed, not the pre-tax total. Does it fit the rule list?
choices: Yes, any change fits any seam
No, it is a different axis
Yes, as a negative discount
items.explanation: It is a different kind of change and needs its own seam.

items.prompt: Each extra stacked if interacts with...
choices: only the last if added
none of the other ifs
every earlier if
items.explanation: That is why the cost of stacking grows each round.

items.prompt: One rule exists. Is the checkout 'extensible'?
choices: Yes, you can always just edit it
No, one rule can never be changed
No, only lists can be extended
items.explanation: With one case, editing is cheap, so no seam is needed yet.

items.prompt: After the seam exists, later rules mostly...
choices: rewrite the checkout loop each time
append without touching the earlier code
need their own brand new seam every single time
items.explanation: That is the payoff the seam was built for.

items.prompt: Round 3 brings (a) a VIP rule that adjusts the total before tax, and (b) EU orders taxed at a different rate. What is the right treatment?
choices: (a) appends to the rule list; (b) gets its own small seam
Both append to the rule list, since one seam already exists
Both get a brand-new seam, because rounds never share seams
(a) gets a new seam; (b) appends to the list as a negative rule
items.explanation: (a) is the same kind as the list's rules. (b) changes how tax is computed, so it is a new axis.
items.reference:
When to add the seam
one rule: plain if
second rule, same kind: add the seam now
second rule, different kind: that is a new axis, new seam
Why: too early is a permanent tax; too late is stacked interactions.
items.learnMore:
Just-in-time seams

Add the seam when the second concrete variant of the same kind appears. A different kind of change is a different axis and needs its own seam rather than a stretched one.

Common mistake

Reusing an existing seam for a different axis. It looks like reuse but recreates hidden ordering confusion.
items.reflection: Think of a tool or system you outgrew. Looking back, at which exact moment did the extra structure start to pay for itself, and who noticed first?

items.prompt: A team added a seam at round 1 to be safe. Two years later the list still has one rule. Which failure is this?
choices: Too late: the second variant arrived long before the seam existed
Too early: a permanent indirection cost for a variant that never came
Wrong seam reuse: the list was forced to carry an unrelated rule
Not a failure: an unused seam costs nothing to keep around or to read
items.explanation: Structure was built without a second variant to justify it.

Immediately, since two small lists are always cleaner than one big one
Never, since a seam may not be reshaped by anyone once it has been created

items.prompt: In the buggy checkout, what did the coupon branch read?
choices: The original subtotal
The already-discounted total
The final tax amount
items.explanation: It restarted from the subtotal.

items.prompt: What happened to the 10% discount when a coupon was present?
choices: It was applied twice
It was silently erased
It was applied after tax
items.explanation: The coupon overwrote the running total from the subtotal.

items.prompt: A $600 order with a $20 coupon in the buggy version: what pre-tax total?
items.explanation: 600 - 20 = 580, with the discount gone.

items.prompt: The same order with correct stacking: what pre-tax total?
What did the buggy version lack?
choices: Enough tests covering the tax step on its own
A stated contract for what each if assumes
A faster way to add up all of the numbers
items.explanation: No block declared what state the running total was in.

items.prompt: In the fixed design a rule receives...
choices: the original subtotal of the whole order
the final total after tax is added on
the running total after all earlier rules
items.explanation: That is the single shared contract.

items.prompt: Where does the fixed design make the business order visible?
choices: In the order of the rule list
In a code comment only
In the tax rate setting file
items.explanation: The list is written in the order the rules run.

items.prompt: Was the round-2 bug a typo?
choices: Yes, a single wrong character in one line
No, shared state with no contract caused it
Yes, a missing semicolon somewhere in the file
items.explanation: The structure invited the mistake, so a patch would not remove it.

items.prompt: Why does the rule list remove the cause of the round-2 bug rather than dodge it once?
choices: A rule receives only the running total, so it cannot read the wrong value
It forces the coupon to run first, so the discount is never reachable
It rewrites the coupon arithmetic so the subtraction is done correctly
It hides the subtotal from every rule, so no rule can see any number at all
items.explanation: The contract removes the choice of which value to read, and with it the mistake.
items.reference:
The $600 order, two paths
subtotal 600, 10% off: 540
coupon reads running: 540 - 20 = 520 (intended)
coupon reads subtotal: 600 - 20 = 580 (shipped)
Why: a rule that receives only the running total cannot read the wrong value.
items.learnMore:
Why the bug was structural

Several blocks shared one mutable value with no contract for what each could assume. The rule list gives every rule the same contract: receive the running total, return the new one.

Common mistake

Treating it as a typo. Patching one line fixes one pair, and the next rule can guess wrong again.
items.reflection: Think of a shared document or spreadsheet where two people each edit from their own copy. Where could one person's work silently overwrite another's, and what contract prevents that?

Writing the rule loop

Each rule is a small function from a running total to a new running total. The checkout loop starts at the subtotal and passes the result along, one rule at a time, in list order.

Common mistake

Reading the subtotal inside a rule. A rule must only use the total it is handed.
